faqs.question: What is Artificial Intelligence?
faqs.answer: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is the simulation of human intelligence processes by machines, especially computer systems. It includes learning, reasoning, problem-solving, perception, and language understanding. AI is broadly classified into Narrow AI (task-specific), General AI (human-level), and Super AI (beyond human).
faqs.keywords: ai, artificial intelligence, define, what is

faqs.question: What is the difference between AI, ML and DL?
faqs.answer: AI is the broad umbrella of making machines intelligent. Machine Learning (ML) is a subset of AI where systems learn from data without explicit programming. Deep Learning (DL) is a subset of ML using multi-layered neural networks. So: AI ⊃ ML ⊃ DL.
faqs.keywords: ai vs ml vs dl, difference, machine learning, deep learning

faqs.question: What are the main branches of AI?
faqs.answer: Main branches include: Machine Learning, Deep Learning, Natural Language Processing (NLP), Computer Vision, Robotics, Expert Systems, Speech Recognition, and Planning & Scheduling.
faqs.keywords: branches, types, areas, subfields

faqs.question: What is the Turing Test?
faqs.answer: Proposed by Alan Turing in 1950, the Turing Test evaluates a machine's ability to exhibit intelligent behavior equivalent to or indistinguishable from a human. A human judge converses with both a machine and a human via text; if the judge cannot reliably distinguish, the machine passes.
faqs.keywords: turing test, alan turing, imitate, human

faqs.question: What is an expert system?
faqs.answer: An expert system is an AI program that uses a knowledge base of human expertise and an inference engine to solve complex problems in a specific domain (e.g., MYCIN for medical diagnosis). It typically consists of a knowledge base, inference engine, and user interface.
faqs.keywords: expert system, knowledge base, inference engine, mycin

faqs.question: What is Natural Language Processing (NLP)?
faqs.answer: NLP is a branch of AI that helps computers understand, interpret, and generate human language. Applications include chatbots, translation, sentiment analysis, summarization, and speech recognition. Core tasks: tokenization, POS tagging, NER, parsing, and embeddings.
faqs.keywords: nlp, natural language processing, text, chatbot, sentiment

faqs.question: What is Computer Vision?
faqs.answer: Computer Vision is a field of AI that enables machines to interpret visual information from the world (images/videos). Tasks include image classification, object detection, segmentation, facial recognition, and OCR. Popular models: CNN, YOLO, ResNet, ViT.
faqs.keywords: computer vision, image, object detection, cnn, yolo

faqs.question: What is reinforcement learning?
faqs.answer: Reinforcement Learning (RL) is a paradigm where an agent learns by interacting with an environment, receiving rewards or penalties. The agent aims to maximize cumulative reward. Key concepts: state, action, reward, policy, value function. Algorithms: Q-learning, SARSA, DQN, PPO, A3C.
faqs.keywords: reinforcement learning, rl, agent, reward, q-learning

faqs.question: What is the difference between supervised and unsupervised learning?
faqs.answer: Supervised learning uses labeled data (input-output pairs) to learn a mapping — e.g., classification, regression. Unsupervised learning finds hidden patterns in unlabeled data — e.g., clustering, dimensionality reduction. Example algorithms: Supervised → Linear Regression, SVM, Random Forest. Unsupervised → K-Means, PCA, DBSCAN.
faqs.keywords: supervised, unsupervised, labeled, unlabeled, difference

faqs.question: What is the difference between classification and regression?
faqs.answer: Classification predicts discrete class labels (e.g., spam/not spam). Regression predicts continuous numeric values (e.g., house price). Both are supervised learning tasks.
faqs.keywords: classification, regression, discrete, continuous

faqs.question: Explain bias-variance tradeoff.
faqs.answer: Bias is error from overly simple assumptions (underfitting). Variance is error from sensitivity to training data noise (overfitting). The tradeoff: reducing bias increases variance and vice versa. Optimal models balance both to minimize total error.
faqs.keywords: bias variance tradeoff, underfitting, overfitting

faqs.question: What is overfitting and how to prevent it?
faqs.answer: Overfitting occurs when a model learns noise in training data and performs poorly on new data. Prevention: more training data, regularization (L1/L2), dropout, early stopping, cross-validation, pruning, and simpler models.
faqs.keywords: overfitting, prevent, dropout, regularization, early stopping

faqs.question: What is cross-validation?
faqs.answer: Cross-validation is a technique to assess model generalization by splitting data into K folds. In K-fold CV, the model trains on K-1 folds and tests on the remaining fold, rotating K times. Common: K=5 or 10. Variants: Stratified, Leave-One-Out, Time-Series.
faqs.keywords: cross validation, k-fold, stratified, generalization

faqs.question: What is regularization? Explain L1 and L2.
faqs.answer: Regularization prevents overfitting by adding a penalty for large weights. L1 (Lasso) adds sum of absolute weights — promotes sparsity (feature selection). L2 (Ridge) adds sum of squared weights — shrinks weights. Elastic Net combines both.
faqs.keywords: regularization, l1, l2, lasso, ridge, elastic net

faqs.question: Explain the confusion matrix and its metrics.
faqs.answer: A confusion matrix shows TP, TN, FP, FN. From it: Accuracy = (TP+TN)/Total, Precision = TP/(TP+FP), Recall = TP/(TP+FN), F1 = harmonic mean of Precision & Recall. Choose metric based on problem (e.g., recall for medical diagnosis).
faqs.keywords: confusion matrix, precision, recall, f1, accuracy

faqs.question: What is the difference between precision and recall?
faqs.answer: Precision = how many predicted positives are actually positive (TP/(TP+FP)). Recall = how many actual positives were correctly predicted (TP/(TP+FN)). High precision → fewer false alarms. High recall → fewer missed cases.
faqs.keywords: precision, recall, difference, sensitivity

faqs.question: How does a decision tree work?
faqs.answer: A decision tree recursively splits data based on the feature that best separates classes. It uses metrics like Gini impurity or Information Gain (entropy) to pick splits. Advantages: interpretable, handles non-linear data. Disadvantages: prone to overfitting → use pruning or Random Forests.
faqs.keywords: decision tree, gini, entropy, information gain, split

faqs.question: What is a random forest?
faqs.answer: Random Forest is an ensemble of decision trees trained on random subsets of data and features (bagging). Predictions are aggregated by majority vote (classification) or averaging (regression). Reduces overfitting and improves accuracy.
faqs.keywords: random forest, ensemble, bagging, trees

faqs.question: Explain SVM (Support Vector Machine).
faqs.answer: SVM finds the optimal hyperplane that maximizes the margin between classes. Support vectors are the closest points to the hyperplane. For non-linear data, use kernel trick (RBF, polynomial, sigmoid). Works well for high-dimensional, small datasets.
faqs.keywords: svm, support vector, hyperplane, margin, kernel

faqs.question: How does K-Means clustering work?
faqs.answer: K-Means partitions data into K clusters. Steps: 1) Initialize K centroids randomly. 2) Assign each point to nearest centroid. 3) Recompute centroids as mean of assigned points. 4) Repeat until convergence. Choose K via elbow method or silhouette score.
faqs.keywords: k-means, clustering, centroid, elbow, unsupervised

faqs.question: What is PCA (Principal Component Analysis)?
faqs.answer: PCA is a dimensionality reduction technique that projects data onto orthogonal axes (principal components) capturing maximum variance. Used for visualization, noise reduction, and speeding up training. Components are ordered by explained variance.
faqs.keywords: pca, dimensionality reduction, principal component, variance

faqs.question: What is gradient descent?
faqs.answer: Gradient descent is an optimization algorithm that iteratively updates parameters in the direction opposite to the gradient of the loss function to minimize error. Variants: Batch GD, Stochastic GD (SGD), Mini-Batch GD. Learning rate controls step size.
faqs.keywords: gradient descent, optimization, sgd, learning rate, loss

faqs.question: What is feature engineering?
faqs.answer: Feature engineering is the process of using domain knowledge to create, transform, or select features that improve model performance. Techniques: encoding categoricals (one-hot, target), scaling (min-max, standard), binning, polynomial features, and text embeddings.
faqs.keywords: feature engineering, encoding, scaling, transformation

faqs.question: How do you handle imbalanced datasets?
faqs.answer: Techniques: 1) Resampling — oversample minority (SMOTE) or undersample majority. 2) Class weights in loss function. 3) Use metrics like F1, AUC instead of accuracy. 4) Ensemble methods (BalancedRandomForest). 5) Anomaly detection framing.
faqs.keywords: imbalanced, smote, oversampling, class weights

faqs.question: What is a neural network?
faqs.answer: A neural network is a computational model inspired by the brain, consisting of layers of interconnected nodes (neurons). Each neuron computes a weighted sum of inputs, adds bias, and applies an activation function. Networks learn by adjusting weights via backpropagation.
faqs.keywords: neural network, neuron, layer, weights, bias

faqs.question: What is backpropagation?
faqs.answer: Backpropagation is the algorithm used to train neural networks. It computes the gradient of the loss with respect to each weight using the chain rule, propagating errors backward from output to input. Weights are then updated via gradient descent.
faqs.keywords: backpropagation, chain rule, gradient, training

faqs.question: What are activation functions? Name common ones.
faqs.answer: Activation functions introduce non-linearity. Common: Sigmoid (0-1), Tanh (-1 to 1), ReLU (max(0,x), most popular), Leaky ReLU, ELU, Softmax (multi-class output), GELU (transformers). Without them, networks collapse to linear models.
faqs.keywords: activation, relu, sigmoid, tanh, softmax, gelu

faqs.question: What is CNN and where is it used?
faqs.answer: A Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) uses convolutional layers to automatically learn spatial features from data. Key components: convolution, pooling, fully-connected layers. Used in image classification, object detection, medical imaging, and video analysis.
faqs.keywords: cnn, convolutional, image, pooling, convolution

faqs.question: What is RNN and its limitations?
faqs.answer: A Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) processes sequences by maintaining a hidden state across time steps. Limitations: vanishing/exploding gradients, difficulty learning long-range dependencies. Solved by LSTM and GRU architectures.
faqs.keywords: rnn, recurrent, sequence, vanishing gradient, lstm, gru

faqs.question: Explain LSTM vs GRU.
faqs.answer: LSTM (Long Short-Term Memory) has three gates: input, forget, output, plus a cell state — handles long dependencies. GRU (Gated Recurrent Unit) has two gates: reset and update — simpler, fewer parameters, faster. GRU often matches LSTM performance on smaller datasets.
faqs.keywords: lstm, gru, gates, cell state, difference

faqs.question: What is the Transformer architecture?
faqs.answer: The Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017) replaces recurrence with self-attention. Key components: multi-head self-attention, positional encoding, feed-forward layers, residual connections, and layer normalization. It's the backbone of BERT, GPT, T5, and modern LLMs.
faqs.keywords: transformer, attention, self-attention, positional encoding, bert, gpt

faqs.question: What is self-attention?
faqs.answer: Self-attention computes a weighted sum of all positions in a sequence, where weights (attention scores) are learned from query-key dot products, scaled by √d_k, then passed through softmax. Multi-head attention runs several attention heads in parallel to capture different relationships.
faqs.keywords: self attention, query key value, multi-head, scaled dot product

faqs.question: What is a GAN?
faqs.answer: A Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) consists of two networks: a Generator that creates fake samples, and a Discriminator that distinguishes real from fake. They train adversarially — the generator improves until fakes are indistinguishable. Used for image generation, style transfer, super-resolution.
faqs.keywords: gan, generative adversarial, generator, discriminator

faqs.question: What are autoencoders?
faqs.answer: Autoencoders are neural networks trained to reconstruct their input through a bottleneck. Components: encoder (compresses), latent code, decoder (reconstructs). Used for dimensionality reduction, denoising, and anomaly detection. Variants: Variational AE (VAE), Sparse AE, Denoising AE.
faqs.keywords: autoencoder, encoder, decoder, vae, anomaly

faqs.question: What is transfer learning?
faqs.answer: Transfer learning reuses a model trained on a large dataset (e.g., ImageNet) for a new task with limited data. Fine-tune the pre-trained model's weights or freeze early layers. Saves training time and improves performance, especially with small datasets.
faqs.keywords: transfer learning, pretrained, fine-tune, imagenet

faqs.question: What is dropout?
faqs.answer: Dropout is a regularization technique where random neurons are ignored (dropped) during each training step with probability p. This prevents co-adaptation and reduces overfitting. At inference, all neurons are used and outputs are scaled appropriately.
faqs.keywords: dropout, regularization, overfitting, neurons

faqs.question: What is batch normalization?
faqs.answer: Batch Normalization normalizes layer inputs across a mini-batch to have zero mean and unit variance, then scales and shifts with learnable parameters. Benefits: faster training, higher learning rates, reduces internal covariate shift, acts as regularizer.
faqs.keywords: batch normalization, batchnorm, covariate shift, normalization

faqs.question: What is a Large Language Model (LLM)?
faqs.answer: LLMs are transformer-based models (billions of parameters) trained on massive text corpora. Examples: GPT-4, Claude, Gemini, LLaMA. They perform text generation, summarization, Q&A, translation, and reasoning. Trained via self-supervised (next-token prediction) then fine-tuned (RLHF).
faqs.keywords: llm, large language model, gpt, claude, gemini, llama

faqs.question: What is RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation)?
faqs.answer: RAG combines a retrieval system (vector database of documents) with an LLM. When queried, relevant documents are retrieved and passed as context to the LLM to generate grounded answers. Reduces hallucinations and enables domain-specific knowledge without retraining.
faqs.keywords: rag, retrieval augmented generation, vector database, hallucination

faqs.question: What is the difference between symmetric and asymmetric encryption?
faqs.answer: Symmetric uses the same key for encryption and decryption (e.g., AES, DES) — fast, but key distribution is a challenge. Asymmetric uses a public/private key pair (e.g., RSA, ECC) — slower, solves key exchange. Hybrid systems (TLS) use asymmetric to exchange a symmetric session key.
faqs.keywords: symmetric asymmetric, encryption, aes, rsa, public private key

faqs.question: What is a man-in-the-middle (MITM) attack?
faqs.answer: A MITM attack occurs when an attacker secretly intercepts and possibly alters communication between two parties who believe they are talking directly. Prevention: TLS/HTTPS, certificate pinning, mutual authentication, and secure key exchange protocols.
faqs.keywords: mitm, man in the middle, interception, attack

faqs.question: Explain SQL injection and how to prevent it.
faqs.answer: SQL Injection occurs when untrusted input is concatenated into SQL queries, letting attackers execute arbitrary SQL. Prevention: use parameterized queries (prepared statements), ORMs, input validation, least-privilege DB accounts, and WAFs. Never trust user input.
faqs.keywords: sql injection, sqli, prepared statement, parameterized

faqs.question: What is XSS (Cross-Site Scripting)?
faqs.answer: XSS injects malicious JavaScript into web pages viewed by other users. Types: Stored, Reflected, DOM-based. Prevention: output encoding, Content Security Policy (CSP), input sanitization, HttpOnly cookies, and frameworks that auto-escape (React, Django templates).
faqs.keywords: xss, cross site scripting, javascript injection, csp

faqs.question: What is CSRF and how to prevent it?
faqs.answer: CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery) tricks a logged-in user's browser into sending unwanted requests. Prevention: anti-CSRF tokens, SameSite cookies, checking Origin/Referer headers, and requiring re-authentication for sensitive actions.
faqs.keywords: csrf, cross site request forgery, token, samesite

faqs.question: What is a DDoS attack?
faqs.answer: A Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attack floods a target with traffic from many compromised machines (botnet) to exhaust resources. Types: volumetric, protocol (SYN flood), application-layer (HTTP flood). Mitigation: CDN, rate limiting, WAF, scrubbing centers, Anycast.
faqs.keywords: ddos, denial of service, botnet, flood

faqs.question: What is hashing vs encryption?
faqs.answer: Hashing is one-way (irreversible) — used for integrity and password storage (bcrypt, SHA-256). Encryption is two-way (reversible with key) — used for confidentiality. Never store passwords encrypted; always hash with salt (e.g., bcrypt, Argon2).
faqs.keywords: hash vs encryption, bcrypt, sha, salt, one way

faqs.question: What is HTTPS and how does TLS work?
faqs.answer: HTTPS = HTTP + TLS. TLS handshake: client hello → server hello + certificate → client verifies cert → key exchange (ECDHE) → session keys derived → encrypted communication. Provides confidentiality, integrity, and authentication.
faqs.keywords: https, tls, ssl, handshake, certificate

faqs.question: What is OWASP Top 10?
faqs.answer: The OWASP Top 10 is a list of the most critical web application security risks. Recent categories include Broken Access Control, Cryptographic Failures, Injection, Insecure Design, Security Misconfiguration, Vulnerable Components, Authentication Failures, and SSRF.
faqs.keywords: owasp top 10, web security, risks

faqs.question: What is penetration testing?
faqs.answer: Penetration testing (pentesting) simulates real-world attacks to find vulnerabilities before attackers do. Phases: reconnaissance, scanning, exploitation, post-exploitation, reporting. Types: black-box, white-box, gray-box. Common tools: Nmap, Burp Suite, Metasploit, Wireshark.
faqs.keywords: penetration testing, pentest, ethical hacking, phases

faqs.question: What is a firewall and its types?
faqs.answer: A firewall filters network traffic based on rules. Types: Packet-filtering (L3/L4), Stateful inspection, Application-layer (WAF, L7), Next-Generation Firewall (NGFW) with DPI. Modern firewalls integrate IDS/IPS and threat intelligence.
faqs.keywords: firewall, packet filter, stateful, waf, ngfw

faqs.question: What is multi-factor authentication (MFA)?
faqs.answer: MFA requires two or more factors: something you know (password), something you have (phone, token), something you are (biometric). Reduces risk from compromised passwords. TOTP (Google Authenticator) and FIDO2/WebAuthn are common.
faqs.keywords: mfa, 2fa, authentication, totp, fido

faqs.question: What is a zero-day vulnerability?
faqs.answer: A zero-day is a vulnerability unknown to the vendor with no patch available. Attackers exploit it before defenders can respond. Detection relies on behavioral analysis, EDR, and threat intelligence. Coordinated disclosure reduces impact.
faqs.keywords: zero day, vulnerability, exploit, unpatched

faqs.question: Explain the OSI model layers.
faqs.answer: The OSI model has 7 layers: 1) Physical (bits), 2) Data Link (frames, MAC), 3) Network (packets, IP, routing), 4) Transport (TCP/UDP, ports), 5) Session (dialog control), 6) Presentation (encryption, encoding), 7) Application (HTTP, FTP, SMTP). Memory aid: Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away.
faqs.keywords: osi model, 7 layers, physical data link network transport

faqs.question: What is the difference between TCP and UDP?
faqs.answer: TCP is connection-oriented, reliable, ordered, with flow and congestion control (used by HTTP, FTP, SMTP). UDP is connectionless, unreliable, unordered but fast with low overhead (used by DNS, DHCP, video streaming, gaming).
faqs.keywords: tcp vs udp, difference, connection, reliable

faqs.question: How does the TCP three-way handshake work?
faqs.answer: Three steps: 1) Client sends SYN to server. 2) Server replies SYN-ACK. 3) Client sends ACK. Connection established. Termination uses a four-way handshake (FIN, ACK, FIN, ACK). SYN flood attacks exploit half-open connections.
faqs.keywords: tcp handshake, syn, ack, three way

faqs.question: What is DNS and how does it work?
faqs.answer: DNS (Domain Name System) translates domain names to IP addresses. Resolution steps: 1) Browser cache, 2) OS cache, 3) Recursive resolver, 4) Root server, 5) TLD server (.com), 6) Authoritative server. Returns the IP. Records: A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, TXT, NS.
faqs.keywords: dns, domain name, resolution, a record, mx

faqs.question: What is DHCP?
faqs.answer: DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) automatically assigns IP addresses, subnet masks, gateways, and DNS servers to devices on a network. Process: Discover → Offer → Request → Acknowledge (DORA). Reduces manual configuration.
faqs.keywords: dhcp, dora, ip assignment, automatic

faqs.question: What is subnetting?
faqs.answer: Subnetting divides a large network into smaller logical subnets, improving performance, security, and management. Uses subnet masks (e.g., /24 = 255.255.255.0) to determine network vs host bits. CIDR notation (e.g., 192.168.1.0/24) is standard.
faqs.keywords: subnetting, subnet mask, cidr, network division

faqs.question: Explain NAT (Network Address Translation).
faqs.answer: NAT translates private IP addresses to public IPs (and vice versa) for routing over the internet. Types: Static, Dynamic, PAT (Port Address Translation / NAT overload). Conserves IPv4 addresses and adds a privacy layer.
faqs.keywords: nat, network address translation, private, public, pat

faqs.question: What is a VLAN?
faqs.answer: A VLAN (Virtual LAN) logically segments a physical network into isolated broadcast domains. Benefits: security, performance, easier management. Configured on managed switches. Inter-VLAN routing requires a router or Layer 3 switch.
faqs.keywords: vlan, virtual lan, segmentation, broadcast domain

faqs.question: What is the difference between IPv4 and IPv6?
faqs.answer: IPv4 uses 32-bit addresses (~4.3 billion). IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses (~340 undecillion), solving exhaustion. IPv6 has built-in IPsec, no NAT requirement, simpler header, and autoconfiguration (SLAAC).
faqs.keywords: ipv4, ipv6, difference, addresses, 32-bit, 128-bit

faqs.question: What is BGP and why is it important?
faqs.answer: BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) is the routing protocol of the internet that exchanges routing information between autonomous systems (ASes). It's a path-vector protocol. BGP hijacking is a major security concern.
faqs.keywords: bgp, border gateway, routing, autonomous system

faqs.question: What is a socket?
faqs.answer: A socket is an endpoint for network communication, identified by IP + port (e.g., 192.168.1.1:8080). Types: Stream (TCP), Datagram (UDP), Raw. Programming: Berkeley sockets API (socket, bind, listen, accept, connect, send, recv).
faqs.keywords: socket, ip port, tcp udp endpoint, berkeley

faqs.question: What is Python and why is it popular?
faqs.answer: Python is a high-level, interpreted, dynamically typed language known for readability. Popular for data science (NumPy, Pandas), ML (scikit-learn, PyTorch), web (Django, Flask), automation, and scripting. Its rich ecosystem and gentle learning curve drive adoption.
faqs.keywords: python, interpreted, dynamic, popular, why

faqs.question: What is the difference between compiled and interpreted languages?
faqs.answer: Compiled languages (C, C++, Rust, Go) translate source to machine code before execution — faster, platform-specific. Interpreted languages (Python, Ruby, JS) execute line-by-line via an interpreter — slower, portable. Hybrid: Java (bytecode + JVM), Python (bytecode + CPython VM).
faqs.keywords: compiled vs interpreted, compiler, interpreter, difference

faqs.question: What is OOP? Explain its four pillars.
faqs.answer: Object-Oriented Programming organizes code around objects. Four pillars: Encapsulation (bundling data + methods, hiding internals), Abstraction (hiding complexity), Inheritance (reusing parent class), Polymorphism (same interface, different behavior).
faqs.keywords: oop, object oriented, encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism, abstraction

faqs.question: What is the difference between a class and an object?
faqs.answer: A class is a blueprint/template defining attributes and methods. An object is an instance of a class with actual values. Example: `class Car` vs `my_car = Car('red', 'Tesla')`.
faqs.keywords: class vs object, blueprint, instance

faqs.question: What is the difference between overloading and overriding?
faqs.answer: Overloading: same method name, different parameters — compile-time polymorphism. Overriding: subclass redefines a parent method with same signature — runtime polymorphism (requires inheritance).
faqs.keywords: overloading vs overriding, polymorphism, compile time, runtime

faqs.question: Explain pass by value vs pass by reference.
faqs.answer: Pass by value: a copy of the argument is passed; modifications don't affect the original. Pass by reference: the memory address is passed; modifications affect the original. C/C++ support both (pointers/&), Java/Python pass references by value for objects.
faqs.keywords: pass by value, pass by reference, pointer, copy

faqs.question: What is a pointer?
faqs.answer: A pointer is a variable that stores the memory address of another variable. Used in C/C++ for dynamic memory, arrays, and low-level optimization. Risks: null dereference, dangling pointers, memory leaks. Modern languages (Java, Python) hide pointers with references.
faqs.keywords: pointer, memory address, c, c++, dereference

faqs.question: What is the difference between a stack and a heap?
faqs.answer: Stack: LIFO, small, fast, automatic (function frames, local variables). Heap: dynamic, larger, slower, manual (C) or GC-managed (Java, Python). Stack overflow vs heap fragmentation are common issues.
faqs.keywords: stack vs heap, memory, lifo, dynamic allocation

faqs.question: What is garbage collection?
faqs.answer: Garbage collection automatically frees memory no longer referenced by the program. Algorithms: reference counting, mark-and-sweep, generational GC. Languages: Java (JVM GC), Python (refcount + cycle detector), Go (concurrent GC).
faqs.keywords: garbage collection, gc, memory management, java python

faqs.question: What is a closure?
faqs.answer: A closure is a function that captures variables from its enclosing lexical scope, even after the outer function returns. Common in JavaScript, Python, and functional languages. Useful for callbacks, currying, and data encapsulation.
faqs.keywords: closure, lexical scope, javascript, function

faqs.question: What is the difference between == and === in JavaScript?
faqs.answer: `==` performs type coercion (5 == '5' → true). `===` checks value AND type (5 === '5' → false). Always prefer `===` to avoid subtle bugs.
faqs.keywords: == vs ===, javascript, type coercion, strict equality

faqs.question: What is recursion? Give examples.
faqs.answer: Recursion is when a function calls itself to solve a smaller version of the problem. Requires: base case (stop condition) + recursive case. Examples: factorial, Fibonacci, tree traversal, quicksort. Risk: stack overflow if base case is missing or depth is too large.
faqs.keywords: recursion, base case, factorial, fibonacci, call itself

faqs.question: What is a Big-O notation?
faqs.answer: Big-O describes the upper bound of an algorithm's time or space complexity as input grows. Common: O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n²) < O(2ⁿ) < O(n!). Used to compare algorithm efficiency independent of hardware.
faqs.keywords: big o, complexity, time, space, asymptotic

faqs.question: What is an array vs a linked list?
faqs.answer: Array: contiguous memory, O(1) random access, O(n) insert/delete (shifting). Linked List: nodes with pointers, O(n) access, O(1) insert/delete at known position. Arrays have better cache locality; linked lists are more flexible in size.
faqs.keywords: array vs linked list, difference, random access, pointer

faqs.question: What is a stack? Applications?
faqs.answer: A stack is a LIFO data structure with push/pop operations. Applications: function call stack, undo/redo, expression evaluation, balanced parentheses, DFS, backtracking.
faqs.keywords: stack, lifo, push, pop, dfs

faqs.question: What is a queue? Types?
faqs.answer: A queue is FIFO. Types: simple queue, circular queue, priority queue, deque (double-ended). Applications: BFS, task scheduling, printer queue, message brokers (Kafka, RabbitMQ).
faqs.keywords: queue, fifo, circular, priority, deque, bfs

faqs.question: What is a hash table and how does it work?
faqs.answer: A hash table maps keys to values via a hash function, offering average O(1) lookup/insert/delete. Collisions handled by chaining (linked lists) or open addressing (linear/quadratic probing, double hashing). Load factor affects performance.
faqs.keywords: hash table, hashmap, collision, chaining, probing

faqs.question: Explain binary search.
faqs.answer: Binary search finds a target in a sorted array in O(log n) by repeatedly halving the search range. Requires sorted input. Variants: lower/upper bound, first/last occurrence, search in rotated array.
faqs.keywords: binary search, sorted, log n, halving

faqs.question: What is a binary tree vs BST?
faqs.answer: Binary tree: each node has at most 2 children. BST: left child < parent < right child, enabling O(log n) search/insert/delete on average (O(n) if skewed). Balanced variants (AVL, Red-Black) guarantee O(log n).
faqs.keywords: binary tree, bst, binary search tree, balanced, avl

faqs.question: What is a heap?
faqs.answer: A heap is a complete binary tree satisfying the heap property: Max-heap (parent ≥ children) or Min-heap (parent ≤ children). Used for priority queues, heap sort, and Dijkstra's algorithm. Insert/delete O(log n), peek O(1).
faqs.keywords: heap, min heap, max heap, priority queue, heapify

faqs.question: What is a graph? BFS vs DFS?
faqs.answer: A graph is a set of vertices connected by edges (directed/undirected, weighted/unweighted). BFS explores level-by-level using a queue — finds shortest path in unweighted graphs. DFS explores depth-first using a stack/recursion — used for cycle detection, topological sort, connected components.
faqs.keywords: graph, bfs, dfs, shortest path, traversal

faqs.question: Explain Dijkstra's algorithm.
faqs.answer: Dijkstra finds shortest paths from a source to all nodes in a weighted graph with non-negative weights. Uses a min-heap (priority queue). Time: O((V+E) log V) with binary heap. Fails with negative weights — use Bellman-Ford instead.
faqs.keywords: dijkstra, shortest path, greedy, priority queue

faqs.question: What is dynamic programming?
faqs.answer: DP solves problems by breaking them into overlapping subproblems and storing results (memoization or tabulation). Requires: optimal substructure + overlapping subproblems. Examples: Fibonacci, knapsack, LCS, edit distance, coin change.
faqs.keywords: dynamic programming, dp, memoization, tabulation, optimal substructure

faqs.question: Compare Quick Sort vs Merge Sort.
faqs.answer: Quick Sort: in-place, average O(n log n), worst O(n²), not stable. Merge Sort: O(n log n) always, stable, requires O(n) extra space. Quick Sort is usually faster in practice due to cache locality.
faqs.keywords: quick sort, merge sort, comparison, sorting

faqs.question: What is a greedy algorithm?
faqs.answer: A greedy algorithm makes the locally optimal choice at each step, hoping for a global optimum. Works for problems with optimal substructure and greedy-choice property (e.g., activity selection, Huffman coding, Dijkstra, MST). Fails for others (e.g., 0/1 knapsack).
faqs.keywords: greedy algorithm, locally optimal, huffman, mst

faqs.question: What is a minimum spanning tree?
faqs.answer: An MST connects all vertices of a weighted undirected graph with minimum total edge weight. Algorithms: Kruskal (sort edges, union-find) and Prim (grow from a node using a heap). Applications: network design, clustering, approximation algorithms.
faqs.keywords: mst, minimum spanning tree, kruskal, prim

faqs.question: What is the P vs NP problem?
faqs.answer: P = problems solvable in polynomial time. NP = problems verifiable in polynomial time. The open question: is P = NP? NP-Complete problems (SAT, TSP, Clique) are the hardest in NP — if one is solved in P, all are. NP-Hard problems are at least as hard as NP-Complete.
faqs.keywords: p vs np, np complete, np hard, complexity

faqs.question: What is SDLC?
faqs.answer: The Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC) is a structured process for building software. Phases: Requirement gathering → Design → Implementation → Testing → Deployment → Maintenance. Models: Waterfall, Agile, Spiral, V-Model, DevOps.
faqs.keywords: sdlc, software development life cycle, phases, waterfall, agile

faqs.question: What is Agile methodology?
faqs.answer: Agile is an iterative, incremental software development approach emphasizing customer collaboration, working software, and responsiveness to change (see the Agile Manifesto). Frameworks: Scrum, Kanban, XP, SAFe. Delivers in short sprints (1-4 weeks).
faqs.keywords: agile, scrum, kanban, sprint, manifesto

faqs.question: Explain Scrum framework.
faqs.answer: Scrum has three roles (Product Owner, Scrum Master, Dev Team), artifacts (Product Backlog, Sprint Backlog, Increment), and ceremonies (Sprint Planning, Daily Standup, Sprint Review, Retrospective). Sprints are typically 2 weeks.
faqs.keywords: scrum, sprint, product owner, scrum master, standup

faqs.question: What are SOLID principles?
faqs.answer: SOLID: S - Single Responsibility, O - Open/Closed, L - Liskov Substitution, I - Interface Segregation, D - Dependency Inversion. These are design principles for maintainable, extensible OOP code.
faqs.keywords: solid, srp, ocp, lsp, isp, dip, principles

faqs.question: What is the difference between MVC, MVP and MVVM?
faqs.answer: MVC: Model-View-Controller (web frameworks). MVP: Model-View-Presenter (view delegates to presenter). MVVM: Model-View-ViewModel with two-way data binding (Angular, Vue, WPF). All separate UI from logic.
faqs.keywords: mvc, mvp, mvvm, architecture, pattern

faqs.question: What is a design pattern? Name common ones.
faqs.answer: Design patterns are reusable solutions to common problems. Creational: Singleton, Factory, Builder, Prototype. Structural: Adapter, Decorator, Facade, Proxy, Composite. Behavioral: Observer, Strategy, Command, Iterator, State.
faqs.keywords: design pattern, singleton, factory, observer, strategy

faqs.question: What is TDD?
faqs.answer: Test-Driven Development (TDD) is a cycle: Red (write a failing test) → Green (write minimal code to pass) → Refactor. Improves design, reduces bugs, and gives a safety net for refactoring. Related: BDD (behavior-focused).
faqs.keywords: tdd, test driven, red green refactor, bdd

faqs.question: What is CI/CD?
faqs.answer: CI (Continuous Integration): developers merge code frequently; automated builds and tests run on each commit. CD (Continuous Delivery/Deployment): code is automatically released to staging/production. Tools: Jenkins, GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, CircleCI.
faqs.keywords: ci cd, continuous integration, continuous delivery, devops

faqs.question: What is the difference between REST and GraphQL?
faqs.answer: REST: multiple endpoints, fixed responses, HTTP verbs (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE), may over/under-fetch. GraphQL: single endpoint, client specifies exactly what fields it needs, strongly typed schema, reduces over-fetching. REST is simpler; GraphQL is flexible.
faqs.keywords: rest vs graphql, api, endpoint, overfetching

faqs.question: What is version control?
faqs.answer: Version control tracks changes to code over time. Git is the standard (distributed). Concepts: commits, branches, merges, pull requests, rebase, tags. Hosting: GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket. Essential for collaboration and history.
faqs.keywords: version control, git, branch, commit, merge

faqs.question: What is the difference between Git merge and rebase?
faqs.answer: Merge: combines branches with a merge commit, preserves history. Rebase: replays commits on top of another branch, linear history, but rewrites commit hashes — avoid on shared branches. Rule: rebase local, merge shared.
faqs.keywords: git merge vs rebase, history, commit

faqs.question: What is a microservices architecture?
faqs.answer: Microservices break an app into small, independently deployable services communicating over APIs (REST, gRPC, messaging). Benefits: scalability, technology diversity, fault isolation. Challenges: distributed complexity, data consistency, service discovery, observability.
faqs.keywords: microservices, monolith, distributed, api gateway

faqs.question: What is code refactoring?
faqs.answer: Refactoring improves the internal structure of code without changing its external behavior. Goals: readability, maintainability, reduce technical debt. Techniques: extract method, rename, remove duplication, simplify conditionals. Covered by tests to catch regressions.
faqs.keywords: refactoring, technical debt, cleanup, extract method

faqs.question: What is unit testing vs integration testing?
faqs.answer: Unit testing: tests individual functions/classes in isolation (fast, mocked dependencies). Integration testing: tests how multiple components work together (DB, APIs). Others: system, acceptance, regression, smoke.
faqs.keywords: unit testing, integration testing, difference, mock

faqs.question: What is HTML and its structure?
faqs.answer: HTML (HyperText Markup Language) structures web content using tags. Basic structure: <!DOCTYPE html> → <html> → <head> (meta, title, links) → <body> (visible content). Common tags: div, span, p, a, img, ul, table, form, input.
faqs.keywords: html, markup, structure, tags, doctype

faqs.question: What is CSS and how does it work?
faqs.answer: CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) styles HTML. Applied via inline, internal <style>, or external <link>. Specificity: inline > id > class > tag. Modern layout: Flexbox (1D), Grid (2D). Media queries enable responsive design.
faqs.keywords: css, styling, flexbox, grid, selector, specificity

faqs.question: What is JavaScript and where is it used?
faqs.answer: JavaScript is a dynamic, event-driven language running in the browser (and server via Node.js). Powers interactivity, DOM manipulation, async operations (fetch/await), and full-stack apps (MEAN, MERN). Standardized as ECMAScript.
faqs.keywords: javascript, js, browser, node, ecmascript

faqs.question: What is the DOM?
faqs.answer: The DOM (Document Object Model) is a tree representation of an HTML page. JavaScript can read/modify it (document.getElementById, querySelector, addEventListener). Frameworks like React use a Virtual DOM to batch updates efficiently.
faqs.keywords: dom, document object model, virtual dom, javascript

faqs.question: What is React and why use it?
faqs.answer: React is a JS library for building UIs with reusable components. Features: virtual DOM, JSX, hooks (useState, useEffect), one-way data flow, huge ecosystem (Next.js, Redux). Maintained by Meta.
faqs.keywords: react, component, hooks, jsx, virtual dom

faqs.question: What is the difference between React, Angular, and Vue?
faqs.answer: React: library, flexible, JSX, virtual DOM. Angular: full framework, TypeScript, two-way binding, opinionated (Google). Vue: progressive framework, template-based, gentle learning curve, reactive data binding.
faqs.keywords: react vs angular vs vue, difference, frontend frameworks

faqs.question: What is Node.js?
faqs.answer: Node.js is a JavaScript runtime built on Chrome's V8 engine for server-side JS. Non-blocking, event-driven, single-threaded with an event loop. Uses npm for packages. Popular for APIs, real-time apps (Socket.io), and microservices.
faqs.keywords: node.js, node, v8, event loop, npm, server

faqs.question: What is the difference between frontend and backend?
faqs.answer: Frontend: what users see/interact with (HTML, CSS, JS, React, Vue). Runs in the browser. Backend: server-side logic, databases, APIs (Node, Django, Spring, Laravel). Runs on servers. Fullstack = both.
faqs.keywords: frontend vs backend, client server, fullstack

faqs.question: What is REST API?
faqs.answer: REST (Representational State Transfer) uses HTTP verbs on resources: GET (read), POST (create), PUT/PATCH (update), DELETE (remove). Stateless, cacheable, uses JSON/XML. Endpoints look like /users/123/posts. Status codes: 200, 201, 400, 401, 404, 500.
faqs.keywords: rest api, http verbs, get post put delete, stateless

faqs.question: What is CORS?
faqs.answer: CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is a browser security mechanism that blocks requests to a different origin unless the server allows it via Access-Control-Allow-Origin headers. Fix by enabling CORS on the server (flask-cors, django-cors-headers).
faqs.keywords: cors, cross origin, browser, security, headers

faqs.question: What is the difference between cookies, localStorage, and sessionStorage?
faqs.answer: Cookies: sent with every HTTP request, size ~4KB, can be HttpOnly/Secure. localStorage: client-only, persists across sessions, ~5-10MB. sessionStorage: same as localStorage but cleared on tab close.
faqs.keywords: cookies, localstorage, sessionstorage, difference, storage

faqs.question: What is responsive web design?
faqs.answer: Responsive design adapts layouts to different screen sizes using fluid grids, flexible images, and CSS media queries. Mobile-first approach: design for small screens first, then scale up with min-width breakpoints.
faqs.keywords: responsive, mobile first, media query, breakpoint

faqs.question: What is a Progressive Web App (PWA)?
faqs.answer: A PWA is a website that behaves like a native app: installable, offline-capable via service workers, push notifications, and HTTPS. Built with HTML/CSS/JS + a manifest.json + service worker.
faqs.keywords: pwa, progressive web app, service worker, offline

faqs.question: What is the difference between SQL and NoSQL databases?
faqs.answer: SQL (relational): fixed schema, tables, ACID transactions, strong consistency (MySQL, PostgreSQL). NoSQL: flexible schema, document/key-value/graph/column stores, eventual consistency, horizontal scaling (MongoDB, Redis, Cassandra).
faqs.keywords: sql vs nosql, relational, document, acid, difference

faqs.question: What is database normalization?
faqs.answer: Normalization organizes data to reduce redundancy and anomalies. Normal forms: 1NF (atomic), 2NF (no partial dependency), 3NF (no transitive dependency), BCNF (stricter 3NF). Over-normalization can hurt performance — denormalize when needed.
faqs.keywords: normalization, 1nf, 2nf, 3nf, bcnf, redundancy

faqs.question: What are ACID properties?
faqs.answer: ACID: Atomicity (all-or-nothing), Consistency (valid state transitions), Isolation (concurrent transactions don't interfere), Durability (committed data survives crashes). Ensures reliable transactions in relational databases.
faqs.keywords: acid, atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability, transaction

faqs.question: Explain different types of JOINs.
faqs.answer: INNER JOIN: matching rows only. LEFT JOIN: all left + matched right (NULLs otherwise). RIGHT JOIN: all right + matched left. FULL OUTER JOIN: all rows from both. CROSS JOIN: Cartesian product. SELF JOIN: table joined with itself.
faqs.keywords: join, inner, left, right, full, cross, sql

faqs.question: What is an index in a database?
faqs.answer: An index speeds up lookups by creating a sorted data structure (usually B-tree) on one or more columns, at the cost of slower writes and extra storage. Types: primary, unique, composite, full-text, partial. Use EXPLAIN to check index usage.
faqs.keywords: index, b-tree, composite index, performance, query

faqs.question: What is a primary key vs foreign key?
faqs.answer: Primary key: unique identifier for each row (not NULL). Foreign key: column referencing a primary key in another table, enforcing referential integrity. A table has one PK, many FKs.
faqs.keywords: primary key, foreign key, constraint, referential integrity

faqs.question: What is a transaction?
faqs.answer: A transaction is a sequence of operations executed as a single logical unit, satisfying ACID. Ends with COMMIT or ROLLBACK. Isolation levels: Read Uncommitted, Read Committed, Repeatable Read, Serializable.
faqs.keywords: transaction, commit, rollback, isolation level

faqs.question: What is sharding?
faqs.answer: Sharding horizontally partitions data across multiple servers (shards) based on a shard key. Improves scalability and performance. Trade-offs: complex queries across shards, rebalancing. Related: partitioning (single server), replication (copies).
faqs.keywords: sharding, shard key, horizontal scaling, partition

faqs.question: What is the CAP theorem?
faqs.answer: CAP states that a distributed system can guarantee at most two of: Consistency, Availability, Partition tolerance. Since network partitions are unavoidable, real systems choose CP (MongoDB) or AP (Cassandra). PACELC extends this idea.
faqs.keywords: cap theorem, consistency, availability, partition, pacelc

faqs.question: What is the difference between MongoDB and MySQL?
faqs.answer: MongoDB: document-oriented NoSQL, flexible schema, JSON-like documents, scales horizontally. MySQL: relational SQL, rigid schema, ACID, joins. Choose Mongo for rapid iteration/unstructured data; MySQL for transactions and relations.
faqs.keywords: mongodb vs mysql, nosql, relational, document

faqs.question: What is an ORM?
faqs.answer: An ORM (Object-Relational Mapper) maps database tables to objects in code. Examples: Django ORM, SQLAlchemy, Hibernate, Entity Framework. Benefits: less boilerplate SQL, portability. Cons: N+1 queries, less control over SQL.
faqs.keywords: orm, object relational mapper, django, sqlalchemy, hibernate

faqs.question: What is a stored procedure?
faqs.answer: A stored procedure is precompiled SQL stored on the database server, callable by name with parameters. Benefits: performance, security, reuse. Cons: vendor-specific, harder to version. Related: functions, triggers, views.
faqs.keywords: stored procedure, sql, function, trigger, view

faqs.question: What is an Operating System?
faqs.answer: An OS manages hardware and provides services to applications. Core functions: process management, memory management, file systems, I/O, networking, and security. Examples: Linux, Windows, macOS, Android, iOS.
faqs.keywords: operating system, os, kernel, resource management

faqs.question: What is the difference between a process and a thread?
faqs.answer: A process is an independent program in execution with its own memory space. A thread is a lightweight unit within a process sharing memory. Threads communicate faster but need synchronization; processes are isolated but heavier.
faqs.keywords: process vs thread, memory, lightweight, shared

faqs.question: What is a deadlock and how to prevent it?
faqs.answer: Deadlock occurs when processes wait indefinitely for resources held by each other. Four conditions: mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait. Prevention: break one condition (e.g., lock ordering). Detection: resource-allocation graph. Avoidance: Banker's algorithm.
faqs.keywords: deadlock, mutual exclusion, circular wait, banker

faqs.question: Explain CPU scheduling algorithms.
faqs.answer: FCFS (first-come first-serve), SJF (shortest job first), SRTF (preemptive SJF), Priority, Round Robin (time quantum), Multilevel Queue. Metrics: waiting time, turnaround, response, throughput. Round Robin is best for time-sharing systems.
faqs.keywords: cpu scheduling, fcfs, sjf, round robin, priority

faqs.question: What is virtual memory?
faqs.answer: Virtual memory lets processes use more memory than physically available by paging data between RAM and disk. Uses page tables and MMU. Enables isolation and larger address spaces. Thrashing occurs when paging dominates execution.
faqs.keywords: virtual memory, paging, page table, mmu, swap

faqs.question: What is paging vs segmentation?
faqs.answer: Paging: divides memory into fixed-size pages (no external fragmentation, some internal). Segmentation: variable-size logical segments (matches program structure, external fragmentation). Modern systems combine both.
faqs.keywords: paging vs segmentation, memory, fragmentation

faqs.question: What is a mutex vs semaphore?
faqs.answer: Mutex: binary lock for mutual exclusion; only the owner can unlock. Semaphore: counter supporting N concurrent accesses; anyone can signal. Use mutex for critical sections, semaphore for resource pools or signaling.
faqs.keywords: mutex vs semaphore, lock, synchronization, critical section

faqs.question: What is a race condition?
faqs.answer: A race condition occurs when multiple threads access shared data concurrently and the outcome depends on timing. Fix: use locks (mutex), atomic operations, or avoid shared state. Example: two threads incrementing a counter without synchronization.
faqs.keywords: race condition, concurrency, lock, atomic

faqs.question: What is a context switch?
faqs.answer: A context switch saves the state (registers, PC, memory maps) of one process/thread and restores another so the CPU can switch execution. Overhead: microseconds. Frequent switches hurt performance; they're triggered by interrupts, I/O, or scheduling.
faqs.keywords: context switch, process, thread, overhead, scheduler

faqs.question: What is a file system?
faqs.answer: A file system organizes and stores files on disk. Provides directories, metadata, permissions, and journaling. Examples: ext4 (Linux), NTFS (Windows), APFS (macOS), FAT32. Key concepts: inodes, blocks, journaling, mounting.
faqs.keywords: file system, ext4, ntfs, inode, journaling

faqs.question: What is the difference between kernel mode and user mode?
faqs.answer: User mode: restricted access, applications run here. Kernel mode: full hardware access, for the OS kernel and drivers. Transitions happen via system calls, interrupts, or exceptions. Prevents apps from crashing the system.
faqs.keywords: kernel mode, user mode, privilege, system call

faqs.question: What is a system call?
faqs.answer: A system call is a programmatic request from a user process to the OS kernel for privileged services (file I/O, process creation, memory allocation). Examples: read, write, fork, exec, open, close. Implemented via traps/interrupts.
faqs.keywords: system call, kernel, fork, exec, read write

faqs.question: What is a finite automaton?
faqs.answer: A Finite Automaton (FA) is a computational model with states and transitions on input symbols. Types: DFA (deterministic) and NFA (non-deterministic). Recognizes regular languages. DFAs and NFAs are equivalent in power; both accept exactly regular languages.
faqs.keywords: finite automaton, dfa, nfa, regular language, states

faqs.question: What is a regular expression?
faqs.answer: A regex describes a regular language using operators like concatenation, union (|), and Kleene star (*). Used for pattern matching in text. Every regex can be converted to an NFA (Thompson's construction) and then a DFA.
faqs.keywords: regular expression, regex, kleene star, pattern, thompson

faqs.question: What is a context-free grammar?
faqs.answer: A CFG consists of terminals, non-terminals, a start symbol, and productions. Generates context-free languages (CFLs). Used in programming language syntax, parsing, and compilers. Parsers: LL, LR, LALR. Pushdown automata recognize CFLs.
faqs.keywords: context free grammar, cfg, cfl, parsing, pushdown

faqs.question: What is a Turing machine?
faqs.answer: A Turing machine is a theoretical model with an infinite tape, a read/write head, and finite states. It defines what is computable (Church-Turing thesis). Languages: recursive, recursively enumerable, and undecidable (e.g., Halting Problem).
faqs.keywords: turing machine, halting problem, computability, church turing

faqs.question: What is the Halting Problem?
faqs.answer: The Halting Problem asks whether, given a program and input, the program will halt or run forever. Turing proved (1936) it's undecidable — no algorithm can decide it for all cases. Proof uses diagonalization.
faqs.keywords: halting problem, undecidable, turing, proof

faqs.question: Explain Chomsky hierarchy.
faqs.answer: Chomsky hierarchy: Type 0 (Recursively Enumerable, Turing machine), Type 1 (Context-Sensitive, Linear Bounded Automaton), Type 2 (Context-Free, Pushdown Automaton), Type 3 (Regular, Finite Automaton). Each level is strictly more powerful.
faqs.keywords: chomsky hierarchy, type 0, type 1, type 2, type 3

faqs.question: What is pumping lemma?
faqs.answer: The Pumping Lemma is used to prove a language is NOT regular (or NOT context-free). Intuition: any sufficiently long string in a regular language can be 'pumped' (a middle part repeated) and stay in the language. Violating this property proves irregularity.
faqs.keywords: pumping lemma, regular, prove, not regular

faqs.question: What is the difference between DFA and NFA?
faqs.answer: DFA: exactly one transition per symbol per state; deterministic. NFA: zero or more transitions, including ε-transitions; easier to design but non-deterministic. Every NFA can be converted to an equivalent DFA (subset construction). Both accept regular languages.
faqs.keywords: dfa vs nfa, difference, deterministic, nondeterministic

faqs.question: What is a compiler's structure?
faqs.answer: A compiler typically has: 1) Lexical analysis (tokenizer), 2) Syntax analysis (parser → AST), 3) Semantic analysis (type checking), 4) Intermediate code generation, 5) Optimization, 6) Code generation. Frontend (1-3) + Backend (4-6).
faqs.keywords: compiler, lexer, parser, ast, code generation

faqs.question: What is Cloud Computing?
faqs.answer: Cloud computing delivers computing resources (servers, storage, databases, networking, software) over the internet on a pay-as-you-go model. Service models: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS. Deployment: public, private, hybrid. Providers: AWS, Azure, GCP.
faqs.keywords: cloud computing, iaas, paas, saas, aws, azure

faqs.question: What is the difference between IaaS, PaaS, SaaS?
faqs.answer: IaaS: raw infrastructure (VMs, storage) — you manage OS and apps (AWS EC2). PaaS: managed platform (runtime, DB) — you deploy code (Heroku, App Engine). SaaS: ready-to-use software (Gmail, Salesforce).
faqs.keywords: iaas paas saas, difference, cloud service model

faqs.question: What is Docker?
faqs.answer: Docker is a containerization platform that packages an app with its dependencies into a portable image. Containers share the host OS kernel (lighter than VMs). Key components: Dockerfile, images, containers, registry, volumes, networks. Compose orchestrates multiple containers.
faqs.keywords: docker, container, image, dockerfile, compose

faqs.question: What is Kubernetes?
faqs.answer: Kubernetes (K8s) is an open-source container orchestration system for automating deployment, scaling, and management of containerized apps. Key objects: Pods, Services, Deployments, ReplicaSets, Ingress, ConfigMaps. Runs on any cloud or on-prem.
faqs.keywords: kubernetes, k8s, pod, deployment, orchestration

faqs.question: What is serverless computing?
faqs.answer: Serverless lets you run code without managing servers — the cloud provider handles scaling and infrastructure. You pay per execution. Examples: AWS Lambda, Azure Functions, Google Cloud Functions. Best for event-driven, bursty workloads.
faqs.keywords: serverless, lambda, functions, faas, event driven

faqs.question: What is blockchain?
faqs.answer: Blockchain is a distributed, immutable ledger of transactions stored in cryptographically linked blocks. Consensus mechanisms: Proof of Work, Proof of Stake. Uses: cryptocurrencies (Bitcoin, Ethereum), smart contracts, supply chain, identity.
faqs.keywords: blockchain, ledger, block, consensus, bitcoin, ethereum

faqs.question: What is a smart contract?
faqs.answer: A smart contract is self-executing code on a blockchain (e.g., Ethereum) that automatically enforces terms when conditions are met. Written in Solidity, Rust (Solana), etc. Immutable once deployed. Enables DeFi, NFTs, DAOs.
faqs.keywords: smart contract, solidity, ethereum, defi, nft

faqs.question: What is quantum computing?
faqs.answer: Quantum computing uses qubits that can be in superposition (0 and 1 simultaneously) and entangled. Enables algorithms like Shor's (factoring) and Grover's (search) to outperform classical computing. Challenges: decoherence, error correction.
faqs.keywords: quantum computing, qubit, superposition, entanglement, shor

faqs.question: What is Big Data?
faqs.answer: Big Data refers to datasets too large/complex for traditional tools, characterized by the 5 Vs: Volume, Velocity, Variety, Veracity, Value. Technologies: Hadoop (HDFS, MapReduce), Spark, Kafka, NoSQL, data lakes, and cloud warehouses.
faqs.keywords: big data, 5 vs, hadoop, spark, kafka

faqs.question: What is Hadoop?
faqs.answer: Hadoop is an open-source framework for distributed storage and processing of big data. Core: HDFS (storage), MapReduce (batch processing), YARN (resource management). Ecosystem: Hive, Pig, HBase, Sqoop, Flume, Spark.
faqs.keywords: hadoop, hdfs, mapreduce, yarn, hive, spark

faqs.question: What is Apache Spark?
faqs.answer: Apache Spark is a fast, in-memory distributed data processing engine. Supports batch, streaming, ML (MLlib), graph (GraphX), and SQL. Up to 100x faster than MapReduce for iterative tasks. Runs on Hadoop, Kubernetes, or standalone.
faqs.keywords: spark, in-memory, rdd, dataframe, mllib, streaming

faqs.question: What is IoT?
faqs.answer: The Internet of Things (IoT) refers to physical devices with sensors and network connectivity that collect and exchange data. Applications: smart homes, wearables, industrial IoT, agriculture, healthcare. Challenges: security, privacy, interoperability, power.
faqs.keywords: iot, internet of things, sensors, smart devices

faqs.question: What is edge computing?
faqs.ans wer: Edge computing processes data near its source (edge devices) instead of a central cloud, reducing latency and bandwidth. Complements cloud for real-time applications: autonomous vehicles, AR/VR, industrial automation, smart cities.
faqs.keywords: edge computing, latency, real time, distributed

faqs.question: What is DevOps?
faqs.answer: DevOps is a culture and set of practices that unites development and operations to deliver software faster and more reliably. Pillars: CI/CD, IaC, monitoring, collaboration. Tools: Git, Jenkins, Docker, Kubernetes, Terraform, Ansible, Prometheus.
faqs.keywords: devops, ci cd, infrastructure as code, culture

faqs.question: What is Infrastructure as Code (IaC)?
faqs.answer: IaC manages infrastructure (servers, networks, DBs) via machine-readable definition files instead of manual configuration. Tools: Terraform, CloudFormation, Ansible, Pulumi. Benefits: versioning, reproducibility, automation, less drift.
faqs.keywords: infrastructure as code, iac, terraform, ansible, cloudformation

faqs.question: What is the difference between AI and machine learning?
faqs.answer: AI is the broad goal of making machines intelligent. Machine learning is one technique to achieve AI — it lets systems learn patterns from data instead of being explicitly programmed. Not all AI is ML (e.g., rule-based expert systems), but modern AI is dominated by ML.
faqs.keywords: ai vs ml, difference, artificial intelligence, machine learning

faqs.question: What is narrow AI vs general AI vs super AI?
faqs.answer: Narrow AI (Weak AI): designed for a specific task, e.g., Siri, chess engines. General AI (AGI): human-level intelligence across all tasks — doesn't exist yet. Super AI (ASI): surpasses human intelligence — theoretical. All current AI is narrow.
faqs.keywords: narrow ai, agi, super ai, weak ai, general

faqs.question: What are the ethical concerns in AI?
faqs.answer: Key issues: bias and fairness, privacy and surveillance, job displacement, autonomous weapons, accountability, transparency (explainability), and concentration of power. Frameworks: EU AI Act, IEEE Ethically Aligned Design, UNESCO AI ethics.
faqs.keywords: ai ethics, bias, fairness, privacy, explainability

faqs.question: What is explainable AI (XAI)?
faqs.answer: XAI makes AI decisions interpretable to humans. Methods: SHAP, LIME, attention maps, counterfactual explanations, decision trees for surrogate models. Critical in healthcare, finance, and law where decisions must be justified.
faqs.keywords: xai, explainable ai, shap, lime, interpretability

faqs.question: What is an agent in AI?
faqs.answer: An agent perceives its environment via sensors and acts via actuators to achieve goals. Types: simple reflex, model-based, goal-based, utility-based, learning agents. Multi-agent systems coordinate several agents (e.g., traffic simulation).
faqs.keywords: agent, rational agent, perception, multi agent

faqs.question: What is heuristic search?
faqs.answer: Heuristic search uses a rule-of-thumb to guide exploration toward promising states. A* uses f(n) = g(n) + h(n) where g is cost so far and h is an admissible heuristic. If h never overestimates, A* is optimal. Examples: Manhattan distance, Euclidean distance.
faqs.keywords: heuristic search, a star, admissible, h function

faqs.question: What is minimax algorithm?
faqs.answer: Minimax is a decision rule for two-player zero-sum games (chess, tic-tac-toe). MAX picks moves maximizing score; MIN minimizes. Alpha-beta pruning cuts branches that can't affect the outcome. Used with evaluation functions in game AI.
faqs.keywords: minimax, alpha beta, game tree, zero sum

faqs.question: What is a knowledge graph?
faqs.answer: A knowledge graph represents entities (nodes) and their relationships (edges) in a structured way. Examples: Google Knowledge Graph, Wikidata, Neo4j graphs. Used in search, recommendations, and question answering.
faqs.keywords: knowledge graph, entity, relationship, neo4j, wikidata

faqs.question: What is fuzzy logic?
faqs.answer: Fuzzy logic handles partial truth (values between 0 and 1) instead of binary true/false. Uses membership functions and rules. Applied in control systems (washing machines, ACs), robotics, and decision support.
faqs.keywords: fuzzy logic, membership, partial truth, control

faqs.question: What is a genetic algorithm?
faqs.answer: A genetic algorithm is an evolutionary optimization technique using populations of candidate solutions. Operations: selection, crossover, mutation. Iterates generations toward better fitness. Used for scheduling, TSP, hyperparameter tuning.
faqs.keywords: genetic algorithm, evolution, crossover, mutation, fitness

faqs.question: What is logistic regression?
faqs.answer: Logistic regression predicts binary outcomes using the sigmoid function to map linear combinations to probabilities. Trained with cross-entropy loss and gradient descent. Outputs interpretable coefficients. Baseline for classification.
faqs.keywords: logistic regression, sigmoid, binary, classification, cross entropy

faqs.question: What is linear regression?
faqs.answer: Linear regression fits a straight line (or hyperplane) y = wX + b minimizing mean squared error. Assumes linear relationship, independence, and homoscedasticity. Extended by polynomial regression and Ridge/Lasso.
faqs.keywords: linear regression, mse, line fit, coefficient

faqs.question: What is the difference between bagging and boosting?
faqs.answer: Bagging trains models in parallel on bootstrap samples and averages (reduces variance) — e.g., Random Forest. Boosting trains sequentially, each model correcting the previous one's errors (reduces bias) — e.g., AdaBoost, XGBoost, LightGBM.
faqs.keywords: bagging, boosting, random forest, xgboost, ensemble

faqs.question: What is XGBoost?
faqs.answer: XGBoost is a gradient-boosting library known for speed and accuracy in tabular data. Uses regularized trees, parallel processing, and handles missing values. Often wins Kaggle competitions. Variants: LightGBM, CatBoost.
faqs.keywords: xgboost, gradient boosting, tabular, kaggle, lightgbm

faqs.question: How do you choose the right ML algorithm?
faqs.answer: Consider: problem type (classification/regression/clustering), data size and quality, feature types, interpretability needs, training time, and inference latency. Start simple (logistic regression, decision tree), then try ensembles and neural nets.
faqs.keywords: choose algorithm, ml selection, decision tree, baseline

faqs.question: What is the curse of dimensionality?
faqs.answer: As dimensions increase, data becomes sparse, and distance metrics lose meaning. This harms KNN, K-Means, and other distance-based algorithms. Mitigation: PCA, t-SNE, UMAP, feature selection, autoencoders.
faqs.keywords: curse of dimensionality, sparse, dimension, pca, tsne

faqs.question: What is a ROC curve and AUC?
faqs.answer: ROC plots True Positive Rate vs False Positive Rate across thresholds. AUC (Area Under Curve) summarizes performance — 0.5 = random, 1.0 = perfect. Useful for imbalanced data. Prefer PR curve if positives are rare.
faqs.keywords: roc curve, auc, tpr, fpr, threshold

faqs.question: What is the elbow method?
faqs.answer: The elbow method picks K in K-Means by plotting within-cluster sum of squares (inertia) vs K. The 'elbow' where the curve bends is a good K. Alternative: silhouette score, gap statistic.
faqs.keywords: elbow method, k-means, inertia, silhouette

faqs.question: What is hierarchical clustering?
faqs.answer: Hierarchical clustering builds a tree (dendrogram) of nested clusters. Two approaches: agglomerative (bottom-up merge) and divisive (top-down split). Linkage methods: single, complete, average, Ward. No need to predefine K.
faqs.keywords: hierarchical clustering, dendrogram, agglomerative, linkage

faqs.question: What is DBSCAN?
faqs.answer: DBSCAN is a density-based clustering algorithm. Groups points in dense regions, labels outliers as noise. Parameters: eps (radius) and minPts (density threshold). Finds arbitrary-shaped clusters; no K required.
faqs.keywords: dbscan, density, clustering, noise, eps

faqs.question: What is anomaly detection?
faqs.answer: Anomaly detection finds rare events or outliers. Methods: statistical (z-score, IQR), isolation forest, one-class SVM, autoencoder reconstruction error, local outlier factor. Applications: fraud, intrusion detection, manufacturing QC.
faqs.keywords: anomaly detection, outlier, isolation forest, fraud

faqs.question: What is time series forecasting?
faqs.answer: Predicting future values from past observations. Classical: ARIMA, SARIMA, exponential smoothing. Modern: Prophet, LSTM, Transformer-based. Steps: decomposition (trend/seasonality/noise), stationarity checks, evaluation with MAE/RMSE/MAPE.
faqs.keywords: time series, forecasting, arima, prophet, trend

faqs.question: What is a recommendation system?
faqs.answer: Recommends items to users. Approaches: collaborative filtering (user-item interactions — matrix factorization, ALS), content-based (item features), hybrid, and deep learning (NCF, two-tower). Cold-start and diversity are key challenges.
faqs.keywords: recommendation system, collaborative filtering, content based, cold start

faqs.question: What is A/B testing in ML?
faqs.answer: A/B testing compares two model versions (control vs treatment) on live traffic to measure impact via statistical significance. Requires sufficient sample size and considers novelty effects. Alternatives: multi-armed bandits, interleaving.
faqs.keywords: ab testing, control, treatment, significance, experiment

faqs.question: What is model deployment?
faqs.answer: Deployment serves a trained model for predictions. Patterns: batch, real-time API (Flask/FastAPI), streaming, edge. Tools: MLflow, TorchServe, TensorFlow Serving, BentoML, SageMaker. Monitor for drift and latency.
faqs.keywords: deployment, serving, mlops, fastapi, mlflow

faqs.question: What is MLOps?
faqs.answer: MLOps applies DevOps to ML: reproducibility, versioning (data + model + code), CI/CD for models, monitoring, and governance. Tools: MLflow, Kubeflow, DVC, Weights & Biases, Airflow, Feast (feature store).
faqs.keywords: mlops, ci cd, mlflow, kubeflow, versioning

faqs.question: What is concept drift?
faqs.answer: Concept drift is when the statistical properties of the target change over time, degrading model performance. Types: sudden, gradual, incremental, recurring. Detection: statistical tests, PSI, ADWIN. Response: retrain, online learning.
faqs.keywords: concept drift, data drift, retrain, monitoring

faqs.question: What is data leakage?
faqs.answer: Data leakage is when information from the test set (or future) leaks into training, giving unrealistically good results. Examples: scaling before train/test split, using target-derived features. Always split first, then transform.
faqs.keywords: data leakage, split, pipeline, leakage

faqs.question: What is feature selection vs feature extraction?
faqs.answer: Feature selection: pick a subset of existing features (filter, wrapper, embedded methods). Feature extraction: create new features by transforming originals (PCA, autoencoders, TF-IDF). Both reduce dimensionality.
faqs.keywords: feature selection, feature extraction, pca, filter wrapper

faqs.question: What is SMOTE?
faqs.answer: SMOTE (Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique) generates synthetic samples for the minority class by interpolating between existing minority points and their K nearest neighbors. Variants: Borderline-SMOTE, ADASYN, SMOTE-ENN.
faqs.keywords: smote, oversampling, minority class, imbalance

faqs.question: What is SHAP?
faqs.answer: SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) assigns each feature an importance value for a specific prediction, based on cooperative game theory. Provides local and global explanations. Widely used for model interpretability.
faqs.keywords: shap, shapley, interpretability, feature importance

faqs.question: What is the difference between parametric and non-parametric models?
faqs.answer: Parametric: fixed number of parameters (linear regression, logistic regression, neural nets). Faster, less data needed, but assumes a form. Non-parametric: number of parameters grows with data (KNN, decision trees, SVM with kernels). Flexible but data-hungry.
faqs.keywords: parametric, non parametric, model complexity

faqs.question: What is quantum machine learning?
faqs.answer: QML combines quantum computing with ML. Approaches: quantum-enhanced classical ML, variational quantum circuits, quantum kernels. Potential speedups for specific tasks but still experimental — current hardware is noisy and limited.
faqs.keywords: quantum ml, qml, variational, quantum kernel

faqs.question: What is federated learning?
faqs.answer: Federated learning trains models across decentralized devices without sharing raw data. Each device computes updates locally; a server aggregates them (FedAvg). Preserves privacy. Used by Google Gboard, healthcare, and finance.
faqs.keywords: federated learning, privacy, decentralized, fedavg

faqs.question: What is few-shot and zero-shot learning?
faqs.answer: Zero-shot: model handles unseen classes without examples (using semantics — e.g., CLIP). Few-shot: learns new tasks from a handful of examples (e.g., GPT prompting). One-shot: single example. Contrast with traditional supervised learning.
faqs.keywords: few shot, zero shot, one shot, clip, prompting

faqs.question: What is self-supervised learning?
faqs.answer: Self-supervised learning creates labels from the data itself — e.g., predict masked words (BERT), next token (GPT), or contrastive pairs (SimCLR). Powers modern LLMs and vision models without manual labeling.
faqs.keywords: self supervised, masked, contrastive, simclr, bert

faqs.question: What is contrastive learning?
faqs.answer: Contrastive learning pulls similar samples (positive pairs) together and pushes dissimilar ones (negative pairs) apart in embedding space. Examples: SimCLR, MoCo, CLIP. Foundation of modern representation learning.
faqs.keywords: contrastive learning, positive pair, negative pair, simclr, clip

faqs.question: What is the difference between AI, ML, DL, and Data Science?
faqs.answer: Data Science extracts insights from data using statistics + ML + domain knowledge. AI is the broad intelligence goal. ML is one approach within AI. DL is ML with deep neural networks. They overlap but emphasize different goals.
faqs.keywords: ai ml dl data science, difference, comparison

faqs.question: What is a hyperparameter vs a parameter?
faqs.answer: Parameters are learned during training (weights, biases). Hyperparameters are set before training (learning rate, batch size, number of layers, regularization strength). Tuned via grid search, random search, or Bayesian optimization.
faqs.keywords: hyperparameter, parameter, learning rate, tuning

faqs.question: What is grid search vs random search?
faqs.answer: Grid search exhaustively tries all combos of hyperparameters (slow, exponential). Random search samples combos randomly (often finds good results faster). Bayesian optimization (Optuna, Hyperopt) is more sample-efficient.
faqs.keywords: grid search, random search, hyperparameter tuning, optuna

faqs.question: What is the vanishing gradient problem?
faqs.answer: In deep networks, gradients become extremely small during backpropagation, slowing or halting learning in early layers. Solutions: ReLU activation, batch norm, residual connections (ResNet), LSTM gates, and better initialization (He, Xavier).
faqs.keywords: vanishing gradient, exploding, relu, resnet, lstm

faqs.question: What is weight initialization and why does it matter?
faqs.answer: Initial weights affect training stability. Poor init causes vanishing/exploding gradients. Methods: Xavier/Glorot (tanh/sigmoid), He (ReLU), LeCun. Modern: default in PyTorch/TensorFlow is usually fine.
faqs.keywords: weight initialization, xavier, he, glorot

faqs.question: What is residual connection (skip connection)?
faqs.answer: A residual connection adds the input to the output of a layer: y = F(x) + x. Introduced in ResNet, it lets gradients flow directly, enabling very deep networks (100+ layers). Used in Transformers and modern CNNs.
faqs.keywords: residual, skip connection, resnet, gradient flow

faqs.question: What is attention mechanism?
faqs.answer: Attention computes a weighted sum of values, where weights come from similarity between queries and keys. Variants: additive (Bahdanau), multiplicative (Luong), self-attention, cross-attention, multi-head. Foundation of Transformers.
faqs.keywords: attention, query key value, self attention, multi head

faqs.question: What is positional encoding?
faqs.answer: Transformers have no inherent order — positional encodings inject sequence position. Original: sin/cos of different frequencies. Modern: learned embeddings, RoPE (rotary), ALiBi. Essential for language and time-series tasks.
faqs.keywords: positional encoding, rope, sinusoidal, transformer

faqs.question: What is BERT?
faqs.answer: BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers) is a pre-trained language model by Google. Trained with masked language modeling and next-sentence prediction. Excels at NLU tasks: classification, NER, QA. Variants: RoBERTa, DistilBERT, ALBERT.
faqs.keywords: bert, bidirectional, masked language model, encoder

faqs.question: What is GPT?
faqs.answer: GPT (Generative Pre-trained Transformer) is OpenAI's autoregressive decoder-only LLM family. Trained to predict the next token. GPT-3/4 power ChatGPT. Enables text generation, code, reasoning, and few-shot learning via prompting.
faqs.keywords: gpt, generative, autoregressive, openai, chatgpt

faqs.question: What is fine-tuning?
faqs.answer: Fine-tuning adapts a pre-trained model to a specific task by continuing training on task-specific data with a small learning rate. Variants: full fine-tuning, LoRA, QLoRA, adapter layers, prompt tuning. Cheap alternative to training from scratch.
faqs.keywords: fine tuning, lora, qlora, adapter, pretrained

faqs.question: What is RLHF?
faqs.answer: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) aligns LLMs with human preferences. Steps: 1) Supervised fine-tune, 2) Train a reward model on human comparisons, 3) Optimize policy with PPO against the reward model. Used in ChatGPT, Claude.
faqs.keywords: rlhf, reinforcement learning human feedback, ppo, alignment

faqs.question: What is a diffusion model?
faqs.answer: Diffusion models generate data by reversing a noising process. Forward: gradually add Gaussian noise. Reverse: a neural net learns to denoise step by step. Power: Stable Diffusion, DALL·E 2, Imagen, Midjourney.
faqs.keywords: diffusion model, denoise, stable diffusion, ddpm

faqs.question: What is CLIP?
faqs.answer: CLIP (Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training) by OpenAI learns joint image-text embeddings. Enables zero-shot image classification via text prompts. Foundation for text-to-image models (Stable Diffusion uses CLIP text encoder).
faqs.keywords: clip, contrastive, image text, zero shot, openai

faqs.question: What is Stable Diffusion?
faqs.answer: Stable Diffusion is an open-source latent diffusion model for text-to-image generation. Works in a compressed latent space for speed. Supports fine-tuning (DreamBooth, LoRA) and ControlNet for guided generation.
faqs.keywords: stable diffusion, latent diffusion, text to image, lora

faqs.question: What is YOLO?
faqs.answer: YOLO (You Only Look Once) is a family of real-time object detection models. Single-pass detection predicts bounding boxes and classes in one forward pass. Versions: YOLOv1 to YOLOv8/v10. Fast and accurate.
faqs.keywords: yolo, object detection, real time, bounding box

faqs.question: What is semantic segmentation vs instance segmentation?
faqs.answer: Semantic: classifies each pixel (car, road, sky). Instance: distinguishes separate objects of the same class (car1, car2). Panoptic: combines both. Models: U-Net, DeepLab, Mask R-CNN, SAM.
faqs.keywords: segmentation, semantic, instance, unet, mask rcnn

faqs.question: What is the difference between CNN and RNN?
faqs.answer: CNN processes spatial data (images) with shared convolutional filters; captures local patterns. RNN processes sequential data (text, time series) with recurrence; captures temporal dependencies. Transformers now often replace both.
faqs.keywords: cnn vs rnn, spatial, sequence, difference

faqs.question: What is the vanishing gradient problem in RNNs and how is it solved?
